summary: The Vickers hardness number calculator turns the force, the mean diagonal length on indentation, the acceleration due to gravity and the length of first diagonal into angle of the pyramid (α). It is built for a lab report, a problem set or a sanity check on a physical situation. The formula is printed further down, so you can check the answer by hand if you want to.

sections.title: How does the Vickers hardness number calculator work?
sections.html:
The Vickers hardness number calculator takes the values in the form, applies the relationship described below and reports angle of the pyramid (α) in the results panel.

Working from the top of the form: you type in the force (F), the mean diagonal length on indentation (d), the acceleration due to gravity (g) and the length of first diagonal (d₁).

Press Calculate once and the page holds the relationship, tracking which boxes you filled and working out everything else; from that point on it follows every edit you make.

Because the equation can be rearranged for each of its variables, the page also runs backwards. Leave the box you want to know empty, fill in the rest, and it solves for the missing one instead. That is useful when you know the answer you need rather than the inputs you have.

  • A measured quantity, entered by default in millimeters. The unit chip switches it to any of the 34 supported units.

sections.title: The formula behind the Vickers hardness number calculator
sections.html:
The page rests on a handful of relationships. Each one can be rearranged for any of its variables, which is what makes the calculator work in both directions:

Angle of the pyramid (α)=2 × ((1 ÷ 2) × vickers hardness number (HV) × (mean diagonal length on indentation (d) ^ 2) × acceleration due to gravity (g) ÷ force (F))
Length of second diagonal (d₂)=-length of first diagonal (d₁) + 2 × mean diagonal length on indentation (d)
Vickers hardness number (HV)=(20000 ÷ 196133) × surface area hardness (H)
Tensile strength (σᵤ)=(10 ÷ 3) × vickers hardness number (HV)

Read it as an ordinary equation. Where a word appears instead of a letter, it is the label of one of the boxes in the form; where a function appears, it is the usual mathematical meaning of that function.

sections.title: What is a worked example?
sections.html:
Suppose Force (F) = 10 N, Mean diagonal length on indentation (d) = 30 mm, Angle of the pyramid (α) = 136 deg and Acceleration due to gravity (g) = 10 m/s². Working through the relationship above gives Surface area hardness (H) = 98.0665 GPa and Tensile strength (σᵤ) = 33.3333 MPa.

Read it as a template. Every number above can be replaced with one of yours; only the relationship between them is fixed.

  1. Enter the values listed above, matching the units each box asks for.
  2. Read off the result. Any field you leave empty is the one the calculator solves for.
  3. Sanity-check the number against the relationship: Surface area hardness (H) = 98.0665 GPa and Tensile strength (σᵤ) = 33.3333 MPa should be roughly the size you expected from Force (F) = 10 N and Mean diagonal length on indentation (d) = 30 mm.

sections.title: What does the result mean?
sections.html:
• Shown in degrees, and convertible to any of the 12 units on that chip.
  • Shown in millimeters, and convertible to any of the 34 units on that chip.
  • Shown in kilograms-force per square millimeter, and convertible to any of the 28 units on that chip.
  • Shown in megapascals, and convertible to any of the 28 units on that chip.

If a number looks wrong, check three things in this order: that the units match what you had in mind, that no drop-down is still on its default, and that the value you entered is on the same scale as the rest — a rate typed as 5 rather than 0.05 is the classic mistake. Those three account for almost every answer that is out by a factor.

sections.title: How are units and precision handled?
sections.html:
Every quantity with units carries a chip beside its box. Switching the chip does not change what you know, only how it is written: values are converted to a common internal base, the arithmetic happens there, and the answer is converted back for display. Mixing metres with feet in one calculation is therefore safe.

  • Force, opening in newtons
  • Length, opening in millimeters
  • Angle, opening in degrees
  • Acceleration, opening in meters per second squared
  • Length, opening in millimeters
  • Length, opening in millimeters
  • Pressure, opening in kilograms-force per square millimeter
  • Pressure, opening in gigapascals

Results are rounded for display but computed at full precision, so chaining one result into the next does not accumulate error. Very large and very small numbers switch to scientific notation rather than printing a run of zeros.

sections.title: When should you use it?
sections.html:
The Vickers hardness number calculator earns its place in the middle of a task, not instead of one. It is most useful when:

  • Solving a problem set where the algebra is more interesting than the arithmetic
  • Testing whether an answer is physically plausible before you trust it
  • Writing up a lab result and needing a quick cross-check
  • Any time the same 4 figures keep coming back — the force, the mean diagonal length on indentation and the acceleration due to gravity — and you would rather not repeat the arithmetic by hand each time.

sections.title: How do you get a reliable answer?
sections.html:
• If a result surprises you, look at the order of magnitude before the digits: a plausible number in the wrong unit looks more convincing than an implausible one, and is easier to miss.
  • Change one input at a time when you are exploring. Two simultaneous changes make it impossible to tell which one moved the result.
  • Keep the units you enter consistent. Mixing centimetres into a field that expects metres is the single most common way to get an answer that is out by a factor of a hundred.
  • Round only at the end. The calculator carries full precision internally, so re-entering a value you already rounded is the fastest way to introduce drift.

sections.title: What else is worth knowing?
sections.html:
• Filling in more than one box is fine. The most recently edited field is the one treated as known, so you can switch direction without reloading.
  • Fields that are still blank are exactly the ones the calculator has not yet been given, so the results panel is a reliable map of what is missing.

faq.q: What does the Vickers hardness number calculator work out?
faq.a: It returns angle of the pyramid (α), derived from the force, the mean diagonal length on indentation and the acceleration due to gravity. Every field in the form feeds the same relationship: press Calculate once and changing any of them updates the result immediately, with no page reload.

faq.q: What do I need to enter to use the Vickers hardness number calculator?
faq.a: The form asks for the force, the mean diagonal length on indentation, the acceleration due to gravity and the length of first diagonal, which is 5 fields in total. Each one is labelled with what it means and, where relevant, the unit it expects. Anything you leave blank is treated as the value to solve for.

faq.q: Can I enter force (F) in a different unit?
faq.a: Yes. Force (F) opens in newtons and the chip beside it offers 16 units. The number you typed keeps its magnitude and only its label changes; the calculation itself happens in a common base unit, so mixing systems in one form is safe.
Yes. Each variable in the relationship can be the one being solved for: fill in the answer you are aiming at, leave the field you want empty, and the calculator inverts the equation for you.

With the values the page starts from, the calculator reports Surface area hardness (H) = 98.0665 GPa. Treat that as a reference point rather than a recommendation: it exists so you can tell at a glance whether your own inputs are on the same scale.

faq.q: Is the Vickers hardness number calculator free to use?
faq.a: Yes — no account, no sign-up and no limit on how many times you run it. The arithmetic happens in your browser, so the values you type are not sent anywhere.
